network.overall_strategy: Construct ten distinct reaction sequences that produce L-alanine as one component of racemic alanine. These include experimentally distinguishable catalyst implementations, not ten independent mechanisms. The network combines Strecker chemistry, five implementations of pyruvate amination, hydroxylamine chemistry, and two thiol-assisted sugar routes. Hydrothermal CO2 reduction supplies a modeled pyruvate source, but its reported micromolar productivity is not silently converted into the millimolar substrate concentrations used in downstream experiments. Cooling into adjacent anoxic porewaters is a conditional transport link; recovery, dilution and reaction rates at those low concentrations remain unresolved. Acetaldehyde, HCN, ammonia, sugar feedstocks, hydroxylamine, reactive minerals and organic thiols are explicit external boundary stocks. Every represented reduction includes its electron donor and an oxidation product. Where mineral oxidation products were not established experimentally, a specific, atom-balanced endpoint is identified as a conditional closure rather than a measured result. Neutral formulas are used for acid-base families; actual protonation follows the stated pH. Both alanine enantiomers are represented separately, and achiral synthesis nodes produce them equally. Enantioenrichment is a separate unresolved module: no reaction is invented that converts D-alanine into L-alanine or produces enantiopure material. CPL can create small excesses, but the supplied evidence does not establish a terrestrial L-favoring irradiation field or sufficiently characterized photoproducts for a closed enrichment reaction (Meinert et al., 2014; Modica et al., 2014). Thus the target is reached molecularly, not as an isolated homochiral product. The environment_formed field records a representative formation setting, not an exclusive location. The intermediate role also covers terminal coproducts because the schema has no byproduct category.

reactions.name: Mineral-assisted hydrothermal CO2 reduction to pyruvate
agents: Awaruite, Ni3Fe, as an H2-activating mineral catalyst

conditions.pressure: 100 bar total as a modeled hydrothermal boundary condition, not a reproduced experimental pressure
conditions.other: Anoxic alkaline rock-water pores, approximately pH 9-11, with sustained H2 supply and dissolved inorganic carbon. The node represents the pyruvate-producing channel, not the entire product distribution. Retain a source concentration ceiling of approximately 10 micromolar before transport losses; do not assume millimolar pyruvate.

reactions.mechanism: Mineral-mediated activation of H2 and CO2 supports reduction and carbon-carbon bond formation. The balanced overall pyruvate channel consumes reducing hydrogen and releases water; its elementary surface sequence is not established.
reactions.reasoning: Preiner et al. (2020) demonstrated H2-dependent inorganic-carbon reduction on relevant minerals and reported pyruvate concentrations up to approximately 10 micromolar across the investigated systems. That upper envelope is not a guaranteed awaruite-specific yield under the modeled pressure. Dilute C3 production is a major network bottleneck. Subsequent chemistry requires cooling into nearby anoxic porewaters, with dilution and adsorption losses retained rather than replaced by an assumed concentration mechanism. Short residence at elevated temperature avoids importing black-smoker conditions into the amination steps (Miller and Bada, 1988).

reactions.name: Strecker aminonitrile formation from acetaldehyde

conditions.other: Anoxic, sheltered aqueous pool; proposed pH 8-9 with ammonia in excess over acetaldehyde. Millimolar aldehyde and cyanide are explicit local feedstock assumptions, not predicted atmospheric concentrations. Limit volatilization and direct UV exposure.

reactions.mechanism: Acetaldehyde and ammonia reversibly form an imine or iminium species; cyanide addition generates racemic 2-aminopropanenitrile. Water is released in the net condensation.
reactions.reasoning: Acetaldehyde-based Strecker chemistry is experimentally established (Strecker, 1850), and Miller's discharge experiments demonstrate formation of alanine from simpler gases through compatible precursor chemistry (Miller, 1953). This node does not assume that a globally reducing atmosphere supplied the required local concentrations. The temperature and pH window is a proposed pool implementation rather than a reproduction of a cited recipe. Insufficient ammonia favors competing cyanohydrin chemistry rather than alanine formation.

reactions.name: Aminonitrile hydration to alaninamide
agents: Hydronium as a regenerated general-acid catalyst

conditions.other: Proposed acidic hydrolysis stage, pH 1-3, in an anoxic chloride-rich geothermal pool. Requires transfer or acidification of the preceding alkaline mixture. Days-to-weeks residence is a scenario assumption; dilute-solution kinetics are not supplied by the research summary.

reactions.mechanism: Proton-assisted water addition to the nitrile, followed by proton transfers, gives the corresponding amide without changing the carbon skeleton.
reactions.reasoning: Nitrile hydrolysis through an amide is the established chemical completion of Strecker synthesis (Strecker, 1850). The specific mild-temperature terrestrial residence time remains an implementation gap; it is not inferred from the mere existence of alanine in discharge experiments (Miller, 1953). Acidic volcanogenic chloride waters provide an oxygen-independent source of acidity. No redox reagent is required.

reactions.name: Alanिनamide hydrolysis to both alanine enantiomers
agents: Hydronium as a regenerated general-acid catalyst

conditions.other: Continue acidic aqueous hydrolysis at proposed pH 1-3 until the amide is consumed, then cool. Released ammonia is predominantly ammonium at this pH; the graph uses neutral-form bookkeeping. L- and D-alanine are produced equally.

reactions.mechanism: Acid-catalyzed amide hydrolysis replaces the terminal amide nitrogen with hydroxyl, releasing ammonia and retaining the aminonitrile-derived stereocenter.
reactions.reasoning: This completes the classical Strecker route (Strecker, 1850). Water and liberated ammonia are explicit, so hydrolysis is atom-balanced rather than represented as unexplained nitrile-to-acid conversion. The original achiral addition produces both stereoisomers; hydrolysis does not select L-alanine. The selected geothermal hydrolysis window is conditional, not a measured rate claim from Miller (1953).

reactions.name: FeS-mediated reductive amination with explicit pyrite-forming sulfur oxidation
agents: Fresh mackinawite as a reactive surface and consumed reagent

conditions.pressure: 100 bar hydrostatic pore scenario; the cited aqueous benchmark does not establish this pressure dependence
conditions.other: Cool anoxic vent-fed porewater, pH 9-10. Iron-route laboratory ammonia benchmarks are approximately 0.375-1.5 M; such concentrations are an unresolved local requirement. Supply at least one external sulfide equivalent per FeS equivalent converted to pyrite. The sulfide node represents the H2S/HS- acid-base pool.

reactions.mechanism: An ammonia-derived imine is reduced while sulfide sulfur is oxidized to disulfide sulfur in pyrite. One FeS plus one external sulfide can supply the two-electron budget per alanine formed.
reactions.reasoning: Huber and Wachtershauser (2003) support reductive amination on freshly precipitated FeS. The specific quantitative pyrite endpoint used here is a conditional, speculative closure because the supplied research does not establish the complete spent-phase inventory. Unlike an agent-only FeS annotation, this node explicitly consumes sulfur reductant and produces FeS2. Its implementation requires verifying pyrite formation and excluding alternative sulfur products. The reported high-ammonia experiments cannot establish the yield from the micromolar pyruvate supplied by rxn_001.

reactions.name: Mixed-valence iron-hydroxide reductive amination

conditions.pressure: 100 bar hydrostatic pore scenario; laboratory benchmark approximately ambient pressure
conditions.other: Anoxic sediment porewater downstream of the hotter source; pH 10; initial Fe(II):Fe(III) approximately 1:1; 72-hour reference duration. A substantial ammonia reservoir is required; the supplied review places earlier iron systems in the approximately 0.1-1.5 M range. Initial ferric material is supplied without invoking molecular oxygen.

reactions.mechanism: Surface-associated pyruvate and ammonia undergo reductive amination. Two ferrous equivalents are oxidized per alanine. Fe(OH)2 and FeOOH provide explicit idealized reduced and oxidized solid inventories; pre-existing FeOOH is retained while additional FeOOH is formed.
reactions.reasoning: Barge et al. (2019) found strong pH and mixed-valence dependence, with the highest reported alanine fraction at pH 10, 343 K and approximately equal Fe(II)/Fe(III). Their approximately 70% value describes detected liquid-phase organics, not automatically isolated yield from all starting carbon. The mechanism and final mineral assemblage were not established. Consequently, FeOOH is a specified, atom-balanced oxidation endpoint for this conditional model, not an experimentally identified unique spent phase. Pure ferrous hydroxide is not assumed to reproduce the mixed-valence result.

reactions.name: Stored Fe0-driven amination on pre-reduced FeS particles
agents: FeS-supported metallic iron inventory supplied as pre-reduced particles

conditions.pressure: 100 bar hydrostatic pore scenario; laboratory amination benchmark approximately ambient pressure
conditions.other: Cool anoxic mineral pore; pH 9.6; 0.5 M total ammonia; 48 hours. The cited experiment used 5 mM keto acid and FeS pretreated at -0.7 V versus SHE for seven days. This network instead declares the resulting Fe0 inventory an external, finite feedstock and does not claim to generate it electrochemically.

reactions.mechanism: An imine-derived intermediate accepts two electrons from Fe0 oxidation to Fe(II). Ferrous hydroxide is the modeled alkaline corrosion product, with water explicitly supplying its oxygen and hydrogen.
reactions.reasoning: Kitadai et al. (2019) demonstrated efficient amination using electrochemically pre-reduced FeS containing metallic iron. The reducing inventory is not a perpetually regenerating catalyst: Fe0 appears as an input and an Fe(II) product appears as an output. Formation of the starting pre-reduced particles under natural conditions remains unresolved and is not hidden inside the agents field. Fe(OH)2 is a conditional alkaline corrosion endpoint, not a claim that it was the only measured product. Near-complete laboratory conversion cannot be transferred to a micromolar hydrothermal feed.

reactions.name: Nickel-catalyzed H2 reductive amination
agents: Metallic nickel on a silicate support

conditions.pressure: 5 bar H2 fugacity; total pore pressure may be higher
conditions.other: Cool, sealed anoxic mineral pore; pH 7-8; 24-hour laboratory benchmark. Low-ammonia comparison uses approximately 6 mM total ammonia. Published screening used 30 mM pyruvate, whereas the internally supplied stream remains at most approximately 10 micromolar before dilution.

reactions.mechanism: Nickel dissociates H2 and hydrogenates an ammonia-derived imine. H2 supplies the reducing equivalents, and water is the net oxygen-containing coproduct.
reactions.reasoning: Kaur et al. (2024) support Ni/H2 amination under mild conditions, including measurable conversion at approximately 6 mM ammonia. This relaxes, but does not eliminate, the nitrogen-concentration problem. Their low-ammonia percentage is referenced to ammonia and must not be compared directly with percentages referenced to pyruvate. Natural exposed Ni0, resistance to sulfide passivation, and maintained dissolved H2 are necessary boundary conditions. The laboratory supported catalyst is not presumed identical to an indigenous mineral surface.

reactions.name: Fe-Ni meteoritic-alloy H2 reductive amination
agents: Exposed Fe-Ni alloy comparable to the tested Aletai meteorite, approximately 18 mol% Ni

conditions.pressure: 5 bar H2 fugacity; total pore pressure may be higher
conditions.other: Anoxic H2-bearing porewater, pH 7-8, approximately 24-hour laboratory comparison. Alloy composition, available surface area and corrosion history must be characterized. An accessible meteoritic metal fragment is an external geological boundary stock, not newly synthesized here.

reactions.mechanism: Alloy-associated nickel activates H2 for imine hydrogenation. H2, rather than unrecorded iron corrosion, supplies the reducing equivalents assigned to this reaction node.
reactions.reasoning: Kaur et al. (2024) observed alanine formation using the Aletai meteorite and substantial accompanying lactate, reported as approximately 24% alanine and 43% lactate in the cited experiment. This is a distinct experimentally tested catalyst implementation, not an independent amination mechanism. Sulfidation, hydroxide coatings and changing alloy exposure may reduce activity. The graph does not borrow additional electrons from alloy corrosion without representing an oxidation product.

reactions.name: Condensation of pyruvate with hydroxylamine

conditions.pressure: 100 bar hydrostatic pore scenario; no pressure-enhancement claim
conditions.other: Anoxic aqueous compartment; proposed pH 5-7 for oxime formation. Hydroxylamine is an explicit external stock, initially at least comparable to available pyruvate. Its source, lifetime and compatibility with dissolved metals are unresolved.

reactions.mechanism: Hydroxylamine adds to the ketone carbonyl and eliminates water, forming pyruvate oxime with unspecified E/Z composition.
reactions.reasoning: Muchowska, Varma and Moran (2019) demonstrated amino-acid formation following hydroxylamine and Fe0 addition to an iron-promoted network. Oxime formation provides the chemically coherent intermediate connecting pyruvate to that reduction. The stated pH and temperature window is a proposed staging choice, not a verified transcription of the primary recipe. Prebiotic hydroxylamine availability is the principal additional feedstock bottleneck.

reactions.name: Four-electron Fe0 reduction of pyruvate oxime
agents: Reactive zero-valent iron surface, consumed during reduction

conditions.pressure: 100 bar hydrostatic pore scenario; no pressure-enhancement claim
conditions.other: Anoxic water; proposed pH 8-9 after oxime formation, allowing ferrous-hydroxide precipitation. Supply at least two reactive Fe0 equivalents per oxime reduced. Carbonate or sulfide capture of Fe(II) would require a different explicitly balanced endpoint.

reactions.mechanism: Reduction of the C=N functionality and cleavage of the N-O bond produce the amino group. Two Fe0 atoms oxidized to Fe(II) supply the four electrons required per alanine; water and Fe(OH)2 close the oxygen and hydrogen inventory.
reactions.reasoning: The hydroxylamine/Fe0 amino-acid route is supported by Muchowska, Varma and Moran (2019). Unlike two-electron imine hydrogenation, oxime-to-amine conversion requires four reducing equivalents; the represented iron inventory supplies them explicitly. The chosen Fe(OH)2 product is a conditional speciation model rather than a verified unique spent phase. No stereochemical selection follows from the achiral reduction.

reactions.name: CO2-dependent cyanide-ammonia conversion of pyruvate through a Bucherer-Bergs-type network

conditions.pressure: 100 bar hydrostatic pore scenario; cited mild aqueous chemistry does not establish this pressure dependence
conditions.other: Anoxic carbonate-bearing porewater; proposed pH 8-9. Ammonia, free cyanide and dissolved inorganic carbon must coexist. Trial boundary stocks of 0.1 M total ammonia and 1-10 mM total cyanide are explicit assumptions, not a verified primary-paper recipe. Separate the fluid from strongly cyanide-binding mineral surfaces. Internally supplied pyruvate remains micromolar or lower.

reactions.mechanism: A lumped formation-and-hydrolysis node represents the reported CO2-dependent hydantoin/carbamoyl reaction network. NH3 and CO2 are listed on both sides because their participation and release cannot be represented correctly by treating them as absent reagents. The fully hydrolyzed neutral-form net is balanceable with cyanide consumption and net CO2 release.
reactions.reasoning: Pulletikurti et al. (2022) support conversion of alpha-ketoacids to corresponding amino acids using cyanide, ammonia and essential CO2. This node does not claim that an atom-balanced sum determines the elementary mechanism or isotopic provenance. Its complete-hydrolysis accounting allows ammonia released from nitrogen-containing intermediates and CO2 released from the combined carbon pools; exact experimental NH3/CO2 fluxes are not established by the supplied summary. Co-location of cyanide with dilute pyruvate, protection from metal complexation, and completion of hydrolysis remain integration gaps. This route is not treated as direct cyanide reduction of pyruvate without CO2.

reactions.name: Thiol-assisted alanine formation from glyceraldehyde
agents: 3-Mercaptopropanoic acid as an organic thiol catalyst

conditions.other: Anoxic, persistently wet sheltered pool; approximately 60 days. Explicit trial stocks: 10 mM glyceraldehyde, 0.1 M total ammonia and 10 mM thiol at pH 5.2. These concentrations and pH are scenario assumptions, not verified values from Weber's 1985 recipe. Shield the long incubation from direct UV.

reactions.mechanism: A lumped low-yield channel involves triose dehydration, thiol-associated carbonyl intermediates and amination with internal redox redistribution. The net conversion releases water and requires no additional external electron donor.
reactions.reasoning: Weber (1985) observed alanine from glyceraldehyde and ammonium, with thiol-enhanced formation of approximately 0.6% after 60 days versus approximately 0.1% without thiol. Those yields are evidence of formation, not predictions for the trial loadings specified here. The net equation is already atom- and redox-balanced; adding an arbitrary reductant would misrepresent the chemistry. Availability and persistence of 3-mercaptopropanoic acid and month-long substrate survival are unresolved prebiotic requirements.

reactions.name: Thiol-assisted alanine formation from formaldehyde and glycolaldehyde
agents: 3-Mercaptopropanoic acid as an organic thiol catalyst

conditions.other: Anoxic sheltered geothermal pool, pH 5.2, approximately 35 days. Explicit trial stocks: 10 mM formaldehyde, 10 mM glycolaldehyde, 0.1 M total ammonia and 10 mM thiol. The temperature, pH and duration follow the supplied report; the concentrations are unvalidated trial assumptions because catalyst loading was not supplied.

reactions.mechanism: Carbon-carbon bond formation accesses C3 carbonyl chemistry, followed by thiol-assisted rearrangement and amination. This lumped experimental channel has the same internally balanced overall oxidation-state redistribution as the triose route.
reactions.reasoning: Weber (1998) reported approximately 1.8% alanine on a formaldehyde basis after 35 days at 313 K and pH 5.2, with little formation without thiol. This is a distinct experimentally demonstrated feedstock entry route, although downstream chemistry overlaps rxn_013. Exact catalyst loading must be checked before quantitative reproduction; the stated trial stocks are not assigned the published yield. Low selectivity, competing sugar chemistry, thiol availability and UV protection remain significant limitations.

reactions.name: Competing H2 reduction of pyruvate to lactate
agents: Metallic nickel or reactive Fe-Ni alloy

conditions.other: Anoxic porewater, pH 7-8, approximately 24-hour comparison. This channel competes directly with rxn_008 and rxn_009, particularly when imine formation is limited by ammonia availability.

reactions.mechanism: H2 activation on the metal is followed by ketone hydrogenation to the secondary alcohol. Hydrogen is the explicit electron donor; no oxygen-containing coproduct is needed.
reactions.reasoning: Kaur et al. (2024) measured competing lactate in Ni/H2 and meteoritic-alloy experiments. The reported product distributions demonstrate why alanine formation cannot be equated with complete pyruvate conversion. This atom-balanced sink uses H2 explicitly rather than treating the metal catalyst as an unspecified source of reducing power.

reactions.name: Competing lactate formation with oxidation of ferrous hydroxide

conditions.pressure: 100 bar hydrostatic pore scenario; laboratory benchmark approximately ambient pressure
conditions.other: Anoxic porewater; pH 7 comparison; initial Fe(II):Fe(III) approximately 3:1; 72 hours. Ferric material is an initial mineral stock, not produced using molecular oxygen.

reactions.mechanism: Two ferrous equivalents reduce the pyruvate carbonyl to lactate and oxidize to ferric oxyhydroxide. Initial FeOOH is retained, and additional FeOOH records the consumed reducing inventory.
reactions.reasoning: Barge et al. (2019) found no alanine under the cited pH 7, 75% Fe(II) condition and approximately 30-50% lactate after 72 hours. This provides a direct selectivity constraint on rxn_006. As in that node, the FeOOH endpoint is a conditional solid-speciation closure rather than an identified unique spent phase; nevertheless, both electron-donor oxidation and all atoms are explicit.

reactions.name: Conditional pyrite-coupled lactate side channel
agents: Fresh mackinawite, consumed together with external sulfide

conditions.other: Anoxic sulfidic porewater, proposed pH 8-10. Relevant when ammonia-derived imine formation is slow. Requires the same verified pyrite-forming redox inventory as rxn_005.

reactions.mechanism: Carbonyl reduction competes with imine reduction while sulfide sulfur is oxidized into pyrite disulfide. FeS, external sulfide and FeS2 explicitly close the two-electron budget.
reactions.reasoning: This catalyst-specific side channel is speculative: the supplied research establishes iron-mediated amination and widespread lactate competition, but not a quantitative pyrite-coupled lactate yield under these exact conditions (Huber and Wachtershauser, 2003; Barge et al., 2019). It is included as a chemically plausible competing sink, not an experimentally calibrated reaction. Its sulfur endpoint must be tested together with rxn_005.

reactions.name: Competing Fe0-driven reduction of pyruvate to lactate
agents: Reactive zero-valent iron surface, consumed during reduction

conditions.other: Anoxic mineral pore; proposed pH 8-9 for the represented Fe(OH)2 endpoint. Competes with amination where ammonia activity or imine coverage is insufficient. No numerical yield is assigned.

reactions.mechanism: Oxidation of Fe0 to Fe(II) supplies the two electrons needed for ketone reduction. Water provides the hydrogen and the oxygen incorporated into the modeled ferrous-hydroxide corrosion product.
reactions.reasoning: Kitadai et al. (2019) demonstrate the importance of metal identity and surface preparation for reductive selectivity. The exact rate and Fe(OH)2 endpoint of this standalone side channel are conditional, not quantitatively established by the supplied summary. It is explicitly balanced and does not use unrepresented proton or electron reservoirs.

pathways.name: Acetaldehyde Strecker pathway
pathways.description: Externally supplied acetaldehyde, cyanide and ammonia form a racemic aminonitrile, followed by staged hydrolysis. Produces L-alanine and an equal amount of D-alanine; hydrolysis conditions and precursor concentrations remain environmental constraints.

pathways.name: Hydrothermal pyruvate with fresh FeS and sulfide
pathways.description: Dilute mineral-derived pyruvate undergoes FeS-associated reductive amination. The represented sulfur-to-pyrite electron closure is conditional and must be verified; no high downstream yield is inferred from the dilute source.

pathways.name: Hydrothermal pyruvate with mixed-valence iron hydroxides
pathways.description: Pyruvate enters a cooler alkaline mineral pore containing both ferrous and ferric components. Ferrous oxidation supports racemic alanine formation, while a shift toward neutral pH favors the lactate side channel.

pathways.name: Hydrothermal pyruvate with a finite pre-reduced FeS-associated Fe0 inventory
pathways.description: Externally supplied pre-reduced mineral particles provide explicitly consumed metallic iron. The route does not assume natural regeneration of the laboratory-prepared reducing inventory or transfer near-complete millimolar conversion to micromolar feed.

pathways.name: Hydrothermal pyruvate with Ni-catalyzed H2 amination
pathways.description: Cooling delivers pyruvate to an H2-bearing nickel interface. This implementation has experimental support at lower ammonia concentrations than many iron routes, but still requires accessible Ni0, sustained H2 and competition control.

pathways.name: Hydrothermal pyruvate with meteoritic Fe-Ni alloy and H2
pathways.description: A reactive Fe-Ni fragment substitutes for the supported nickel catalyst. This experimentally distinct implementation shares the H2 reductive-amination mechanism and can produce substantial lactate alongside both alanine enantiomers.

pathways.name: Pyruvate oxime formation followed by Fe0 reduction
pathways.description: An external hydroxylamine stock converts pyruvate to its oxime. Explicit four-electron reduction by metallic iron yields racemic alanine. Hydroxylamine availability and the required staging of aqueous conditions are additional bottlenecks.

pathways.name: CO2-dependent cyanide-ammonia pathway from pyruvate
pathways.description: Pyruvate enters a separate carbonate-, cyanide- and ammonia-bearing reaction compartment. A lumped Bucherer-Bergs-type formation-and-hydrolysis node reaches racemic alanine; co-location, mineral compatibility and complete hydrolysis are not assumed demonstrated.

pathways.name: Glyceraldehyde-thiol pathway
pathways.description: Externally supplied racemic glyceraldehyde and ammonium undergo a slow thiol-assisted net conversion. The reported low-yield route produces L-alanine within a racemate without cyanide or an added external reductant.

pathways.name: Formaldehyde-glycolaldehyde-thiol pathway
pathways.description: Externally supplied C1 and C2 aldehydes enter a demonstrated thiol-assisted C3 assembly and amination channel. It is distinct from direct glyceraldehyde feeding, although downstream chemistry overlaps that route.

pathway_evaluations.feedback: This is the strongest complete route from the declared boundary stocks. Acetaldehyde Strecker chemistry and hydrolysis through alaninamide are well established in the supplied literature. Racemic alanine contains the requested L-alanine, so lack of enantioenrichment does not invalidate the stated target achievement. The principal uncertainty is environmental implementation: the Surface label does not specify the pH, temperature or residence time needed for nitrile and amide hydrolysis. Aminonitrile formation alone does not establish efficient free-alanine production.
suggestions: Specify pH, temperature and residence time separately for aminonitrile formation, hydration and amide hydrolysis, including any justified changes between them.
Represent mol_008 and mol_009 explicitly as racemic pools and attach reaction-specific experimental citations.
Account for cyanohydrin formation and competing lactate production when estimating alanine yield.

pathway_evaluations.feedback: The supplied Preiner et al. (2020) findings support mineral-assisted CO2/H2 production of trace pyruvate, while Huber and Wachtershauser (2003) support FeS-associated reductive amination. These do not establish the combined pathway at transported micromolar pyruvate concentrations. The explicit FeS/H2S-to-pyrite accounting is a plausible conditional redox closure, not a demonstrated mineral endpoint for this implementation. The corresponding pyrite-coupled lactate channel, rxn_017, is less directly supported than the general observation of competing lactate formation.
suggestions: Identify the actual upstream catalyst and conditions; generic mineral assistance does not establish equivalence to greigite, magnetite or awaruite experiments.
Specify fresh FeS preparation or supply, sulfide activity, ammonia concentration, pH and temperature for rxn_005.
Measure mineral oxidation products and substrate selectivity before treating pyrite formation as experimentally established.
Test amination after realistic cooling and dilution, rather than importing yields measured with millimolar pyruvate.

pathway_evaluations.feedback: Barge et al. (2019) directly support alanine and lactate formation in mixed-valence iron hydroxide systems. Including both products is appropriate. However, activity depends strongly on pH and mineral oxidation state; the results cannot be generalized to arbitrary mixtures of Fe(OH)2 and FeOOH. The stated ferric oxyhydroxide endpoint is a conditional representation of mineral oxidation, not a resolved experimental mechanism. Cooling is physically plausible, but substrate recovery and downstream performance at micromolar pyruvate remain unverified.
suggestions: Specify mineral phase, Fe(II):Fe(III) ratio, ammonia concentration and reaction time; distinguish the alkaline alanine-producing conditions from lower-pH lactate-favoring conditions.
Track initial Fe(III) separately from Fe(III) generated by oxidation of the ferrous reductant, using explicit stoichiometric coefficients.
Validate the cooled-feed experiment without equating the reported liquid-phase product proportions with overall carbon recovery.

pathway_evaluations.feedback: The supplied Kitadai et al. (2019) findings support reductive amination using pre-reduced FeS containing Fe0. Treating the reducing capacity as a finite supplied inventory avoids implying an unexplained sustained electrochemical input. Nevertheless, isolated Fe0 in the reaction equation does not fully specify the experimentally active FeS-associated material. Fe(OH)2 is an acceptable conditional accounting endpoint, but its actual formation and persistence depend on porewater composition. Upstream pyruvate delivery and the high-ammonia reaction environment remain conditional.
suggestions: Specify the Fe0 loading, accessible reducing capacity, FeS support and passivation behavior of the supplied material.
Define an aqueous environment consistent with the reported approximately room-temperature, pH 9.6, ammonia-rich experiments, or justify departures experimentally.
Measure iron oxidation products and alanine/lactate partitioning at the actual transported pyruvate concentration.

pathway_evaluations.feedback: Kaur et al. (2024) provide strong experimental support for nickel-catalyzed H2 reductive amination and competing lactate formation. The explicit hydrogen donor and water product correctly describe the net amination. The environmental case still requires a specified nickel catalyst, maintained hydrogen activity and appropriate ammonia availability. Results obtained with a supported laboratory catalyst at 5 bar H2 do not automatically establish performance on an unspecified natural nickel surface. The hydrothermal-to-porewater concentration mismatch is acknowledged but unresolved.
suggestions: Specify nickel oxidation state, support, loading and accessible surface area, distinguishing demonstrated catalyst formulations from proposed natural equivalents.
Define how the cooled compartment maintains the reported near-neutral pH, approximately 22 degrees C and sufficient H2 pressure or dissolved activity.
Measure selectivity and rate at micromolar pyruvate, retaining rxn_015 as a competing sink.

pathway_evaluations.feedback: The meteoritic-alloy implementation has direct support from the Aletai experiment reported by Kaur et al. (2024), making it more than a speculative substitution for nickel. That experiment also produced substantial lactate, so the included competing sink is important. A supplied alloy stock is a legitimate boundary condition, but its composition, corrosion state and catalytic accessibility must be specified. The network does not yet establish coexistence of an active alloy surface, sufficient H2 and recoverable hydrothermal pyruvate under the proposed porewater conditions.
suggestions: Specify an experimentally comparable alloy composition, exposed metal area and weathering state.
Retain the reported alanine/lactate competition rather than transferring selectivity from a different nickel catalyst.
Quantify H2 availability, transport losses and alloy performance at the downstream substrate concentration.

pathway_evaluations.feedback: Oxime formation followed by Fe0 reduction is chemically coherent and supported by the supplied Muchowska, Varma and Moran (2019) findings. Correctly treating oxime-to-alanine conversion as a four-electron reduction is a strength. Hydroxylamine is explicitly supplied, so its synthesis need not be invented within this network; nevertheless, its concentration and survival in the proposed compartment require specification. The exact iron oxidation endpoint and performance with dilute hydrothermal pyruvate remain conditional.
suggestions: Specify hydroxylamine concentration, pH, temperature and oxime formation time, including competing hydroxylamine consumption.
Document Fe0 loading and passivation, and verify the assumed Fe(II) product rather than treating Fe(OH)2 as measured.
Test the sequential condensation and reduction using realistically recovered hydrothermal feed.

pathway_evaluations.feedback: Pulletikurti et al. (2022) support cyanide/ammonia/CO2-enabled conversion of alpha-ketoacids to amino acids. Thus the transformation has experimental grounding, but rxn_012 compresses a multistep network whose intermediate processing and atom mapping are not documented here. The deterministic balanceability result is accepted. Because NH3 and CO2 occur on both sides, explicit coefficients are needed to distinguish initial reagent pools from net production or consumption; their repeated presence alone does not establish the redox mechanism.
suggestions: Document the hydantoin and N-carbamoyl intermediates and the conditions that release free alanine, either as substeps or in reaction reasoning.
Specify net CO2 production and carbon/nitrogen fate with explicit coefficients; a formally balanced overall equation is not an experimentally established atom map.
Define cyanide, ammonia and inorganic-carbon activities and test the conversion at the transported pyruvate concentration.

pathway_evaluations.feedback: Weber (1985) experimentally supports low-yield alanine formation from glyceraldehyde and ammonium, accelerated by an organic thiol. The net reaction is chemically plausible through internal redox redistribution and does not inherently require an omitted external reductant. This route independently reaches racemic alanine from declared boundary stocks. Its main implementation uncertainties are the unspecified thiol, long residence time and substrate/catalyst survival. The reported approximately 0.6% outcome after 60 days supports occurrence, not rapid or selective conversion.
suggestions: Specify the demonstrated thiol identity, such as 3-mercaptopropionic acid, its loading and its availability as a boundary stock.
Define pH, temperature and a physically justified residence time consistent with the glyceraldehyde experiment.
Annotate the lumped mechanism and quantify lactate and other competing products without presenting the net equation as a single elementary step.

pathway_evaluations.feedback: Weber (1998) directly supports thiol-assisted alanine formation from formaldehyde, glycolaldehyde and ammonia. The supplied literature reports approximately 1.8% alanine on a formaldehyde basis after 35 days at pH 5.2 and 40 degrees C. Those results support molecular target production, while the low yield does not itself make the route invalid. The Surface designation remains insufficient to verify sustained experimental conditions, thiol persistence or protection from competing aldehyde chemistry.
suggestions: Specify the thiol identity and loading, substrate concentrations and conditions corresponding to the cited experiment.
Provide a credible aqueous residence-time and replenishment model for the month-long reaction.
Track competing products and preserve the reported formaldehyde-based yield definition when estimating L-alanine output.

evaluation.network_feedback: This is a connected, chemically credible proposed network, but not yet a demonstrated integrated environmental synthesis system. All 23 molecule nodes and 18 reaction nodes participate in the connected graph, and molecule IDs are used consistently. Accepting the deterministic check as ground truth, there are no conservation violations: all reactions are balanced or balanceable. Explicit stoichiometric coefficients should nevertheless be stored, especially where mineral or inorganic-carbon species occur on both sides. The underlying reaction families align well with the supplied literature. Strengths include explicit reducing equivalents, separate L/D products, competing lactate channels, finite Fe0 inventories and honest separation of measured results from conditional mineral endpoints. Racemic production achieves the expressly stated molecular L-alanine target; it does not establish enrichment or isolation, neither of which is claimed. The main limitations are missing reaction-specific environmental parameters and catalyst specifications, unresolved recovery and kinetics between micromolar hydrothermal pyruvate production and downstream amination, and incompletely validated mineral endpoints. In particular, rxn_017 should remain a hypothesis rather than an experimentally established side reaction. Declared external stocks are legitimate boundaries, but their local concentrations and persistence need specification. Reaction-linked primary citations should be added; the extensive supplied research does not replace that traceability. Listed problematic reactions denote these chemical or implementation uncertainties, not atom-balance failures.
